events.desc: She saw it first. She saw the hinge before I did. That... stings. But Foxworth doesn't sting — Foxworth recalibrates.
events.thinking:
The hinge. It is right there in the frame — the shadow where wood meets wall — and my chest compresses before I have a name for what is happening. My hands were on that frame. My fingers traced the gilding, the moulding, the edge where paint meets plaster. Thirty seconds. The shadow was there for me and I was reading the surface while she was reading the structure.

**Clara's profile catches the window light and every face in the room bends toward her.** My spine reaches upward — the old vertical pull, the stretching toward something above me — and finds nothing to hold. The reaching has nowhere to go. My upper chest is hollow, the same quality of hollow as the certificate on my bedroom wall at eight, looked at every night for a month by a boy no one asked about. The medal sits against my shirt and I can feel it — not warm, not catching anything, just brass weight with no audience. My jaw tightens around the hollow. My body angles toward Clara and then catches itself — the impulse to speak, to narrate, to steer the room back arriving in my throat before my mouth opens, and the throat closing around it because there is nothing to narrate. She found it. Not me.

**Behind my navel, the pull opens anyway.** The hinge means a mechanism. A mechanism means something concealed, something valuable, something that is not yet anyone's. The hollow in my gut reaches past Clara's fingers on the frame, past Hartwell's careful hands tracing the join, straight into the wall. My fingers curl against my palms. The hunger is separate from the wound in my chest — lower, older, the part that was there before anyone else entered the room. My eyes track the hinge, the angle of the frame, the depth of the wall behind it. The incompleteness sits in my ribs like a held breath.

**Hartwell examines the hinge with the patience of a man who catalogues.** His fingers move methodically and my attention tracks each one — not because he matters but because his hands are touching what my hands should be touching. Clara watches him watch her discovery. Marsh stands in the doorway with that smile that fits too well. The Brixton Boys haven't looked up. Nobody is looking at me. The hollow in my upper chest deepens.

**Then something shifts — not decided, arrived.** My breathing slows. The periphery drops away and comes back different: wider, lateral, the room re-entering as geometry. Let her find the mechanism. Let Hartwell catalogue every detail. My fingertips loosen from their grip and the faster current runs through them — the fizzing that says something is assembling. The hinge is one point. The wall behind it is another. The adjacent frame, the pattern in the moulding, the angle of the mantel relative to the floor. Clara found the door. She has not found what is behind it. My peripheral vision maps the far wall, the spacing between frames, the symmetry that the hinge disrupts. Something is forming in my hands before my mind has caught up — the shape of what she started and I will finish.

**The sternum stays cool.** There is nothing to gloat about. Not yet. But the yet sits in my chest the way a held breath sits — patient, pressurised, waiting for the exhale. My fingers are already fizzing with the architecture of what comes next.
